segment_name: A Woman Stripped of Everything: Opening on Magdalen's Dispossession

questions.question: Oliver, you've said that the moment Mr. Vanstone recognises his daughter as a woman is basically a physiological catastrophe — that Collins encodes it into the body before language even gets a chance to intervene. That passage: 'the trouble of her bosom pressed against his; in the nervous thrill of her arms clasped around his neck' — what is it actually doing to us when we read it? Because it feels almost unbearable.
questions.intent: Draw out Trevelyan's strongest take on the tactile encoding of sexual recognition and the way syntax bypasses readerly defence — sets up the scene viscerally before the others reframe it politically or economically

questions.question: Edmund, you heard Oliver describe that same moment as a kind of syntactic rupture — the body registering what the father's mind refuses to. But you've framed it very differently: you've said what's really happening there is that Mr. Vanstone's innocence has been an act of prolonged infantilisation, that he's been denying Magdalen personhood for years before the law gets round to doing it officially. Can those two readings live together, or does one of them have to be wrong?
questions.intent: Set up a direct, productive tension between Trevelyan's physiological-syntactic reading and Leigh's moral-philosophical one — forces both to sharpen their positions

questions.question: Daniel, you've been quiet on the father — your attention is really on what Magdalen says next, in that oath she swears in Chapter 16: 'He shall never marry me till I can be what my father said I should be — the making of his fortune.' You've described that as the novel's central economic tragedy. But here's what I want to push on: she sounds genuinely noble there. She sounds like someone making a real promise. Are you saying that nobility is itself the trap?
questions.intent: Get Rosen to articulate his most counterintuitive claim — that Magdalen's apparent virtue is a symptom of structural entrapment, not a moral achievement — and provoke Leigh, who reads the oath as sincere rather than symptomatic

questions.question: Edmund, Daniel is essentially saying the happy ending is a tragedy in disguise — that Magdalen marrying Kirke is just the law winning, domestication dressed up as redemption. You've argued the opposite: that her refusing the inheritance money she fought for proves she chose redemption rather than being crushed. But doesn't Daniel have a point? If the only exit from dispossession is a husband, is that really a choice?
questions.intent: Force the sharpest disagreement of the segment — Leigh's moral-agency reading versus Rosen's structural-entrapment reading of the ending — and get Trevelyan to weigh in on whether the brevity of 'Neither you nor I are fit to speak of her' reads as redemption or shutdown

questions.question: Oliver, let's end on that final line you flagged — 'Say nothing about my sister! Neither you nor I are fit to speak of her.' You've said the em-dash is the real confession, that it's Magdalen dropping the performance entirely. But Edmund hears moral self-recognition there, and Daniel hears the law's contamination — the way working toward independence makes a woman feel criminal even when she isn't. When you read that line aloud in your head, what do you actually hear?
questions.intent: Close the segment on a moment of genuine interpretive openness — inviting all three to converge on the same passage from their different angles, with Trevelyan's performative ear as the anchor, and producing the kind of quiet, revelatory radio moment that follows a good argument

steering_notes: The segment should move from body to language to law — Trevelyan opens the visceral register, Leigh lifts it into moral philosophy, Rosen grounds it in statute. The risk is that Rosen's materialist reading comes across as reductive; push him to make it feel as emotionally alive as the others. The strongest moment will be when all three land on that final em-dash passage and realise they're describing completely different silences. Keep it warm and argumentative — these three genuinely disagree about whether Magdalen has any agency at all, which is exactly where the energy is.

segment_name: The Comedy of Survival: Wragge's World and the Masks We Wear

questions.question: Oliver, you've argued that Wragge isn't just a funny con-man who happens to wear disguises — he's Collins actually working out a theory of identity, that the self is performed rather than possessed. But here's what I want to push on: when Wragge explains his own methods, does he read as someone who *knows* that, or is Collins the one who knows it and Wragge is just the vehicle?
questions.intent: Draw out Trevelyan's strongest claim that Wragge is a deliberate philosophical project, not comic relief — and open the door for Leigh and Rosen to complicate whether 'performed identity' is liberating or just a survival necessity

questions.question: Edmund, there's that extraordinary passage where Norah — who has done nothing, schemed nothing, stooped to nothing — ends up with exactly what Magdalen nearly destroyed herself trying to get. Collins seems to be saying the quiet part loud: virtue didn't win, *luck* won. Does the novel actually believe that, or is it hedging?
questions.intent: Get Leigh to articulate the moral luck argument directly and quote the Norah passage — then set up Rosen to reframe 'luck' as 'legal structure' and Trevelyan to ask whether performance is the only rational response to a world where virtue is useless

questions.question: Daniel, you've said something that I think would genuinely surprise a lot of readers — that Mrs. Lecount and Mrs. Wragge aren't really villainous or comic, they're *workers* whose entire economic survival is contingent on not being found out. If that's right, what do we do with the comedy? Are we laughing at people in genuinely desperate situations and just not noticing?
questions.intent: Force the uncomfortable question about whether the novel's comic register is ideologically complicit — and invite Trevelyan to defend the comedy as meaningful and Leigh to argue that the desperation is the point, not a hidden subtext

questions.question: Here's a provocation for the table: Magdalen lies, schemes, disguises herself, nearly breaks — and Edmund, you've said she's *more honest* than Norah, who just resigns herself and gets lucky. Oliver, you think the performance is the whole point. But Daniel, you've said her scheming isn't free brilliance, it's constrained desperation. So is Magdalen a heroine, a symptom, or both — and does the novel know the difference?
questions.intent: Create a three-way collision on Magdalen's agency — Trevelyan defending the theatrical self as meaningful, Leigh arguing virtue ethics has collapsed so 'heroine' is a category error, Rosen insisting she has three economic options and none of them are freedom

questions.question: Last one, and I want to end on this: Collins was a playwright, a collaborator with Dickens, someone who spent years thinking about performance as craft. Oliver, you've argued that background is *constitutive* — that he couldn't have written Wragge without it. But if the novel's also doing what Edmund and Daniel are describing — diagnosing a society where you *have* to perform to survive — does Collins's theatrical delight in disguise sit comfortably with that darker argument, or is there a tension there he never quite resolves?
questions.intent: Close the segment by asking whether Collins's theatrical joy and his social critique are in tension — get Trevelyan to defend the synthesis, Leigh to argue the comedy is part of the diagnosis, and leave the audience with a genuinely open question

steering_notes: This segment has strong potential for productive three-way friction: Trevelyan celebrates performance as meaningful, Leigh sees it as evidence that virtue ethics has collapsed, and Rosen insists the whole frame is economically determined. Let those tensions develop — don't rush to synthesis. The comedy question is the emotional core: we need to get the panel to sit with the discomfort that we've been laughing at people with nowhere else to go. Keep energy warm but push back when anyone reaches for easy resolution — the novel doesn't offer one.

segment_name: Victorian Property and Powerlessness: What No Name Really Means

questions.question: Edmund, you've argued that Magdalen's psychological collapse isn't something that happens *because* she schemes — it's already underway before the scheming starts. The crime is the symptom, not the cause. Can you take us into that passage where she says 'I am nothing to myself; I am no more interested in myself than I am in these handfuls of grass' — what is Collins doing there, and why does it matter that the dissolution comes *first*?
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's central thesis about legal non-personhood preceding and authorizing psychological annihilation; anchor the argument in the specific passage and its grammatical movement from assertion to negation

questions.question: Oliver, you've been listening to the rhythm of these passages, and you've noticed something interesting — that phrase 'I have lost all care for myself' keeps coming back across the novel like a stuck record. You've argued that's not sloppy writing, that's trauma working in the body. But here's my question: does that repetition belong to Magdalen, or does it belong to Collins? Is he giving her a voice, or is he performing her dissolution *for* her?
questions.intent: Push Trevelyan to commit to his strongest claim about prose enacting psychological fragmentation, and open a productive tension with Leigh's legal-philosophical reading by raising the question of authorial control versus character interiority

questions.question: Daniel, you've done the maths on this — Magdalen's annual earning capacity from acting is somewhere around a hundred to a hundred and fifty pounds, set against a Vanstone fortune yielding three to five thousand a year. That's a ratio of roughly one to thirty. So here's a blunt question: when she says 'I have only one end in life now, and the sooner I reach it and die the better' — is that a woman in moral freefall, or is that a woman who has correctly calculated her own economic situation?
questions.intent: Let Rosen detonate his strongest materialist argument — that her despair is rational economic recognition, not interior neurosis — and directly challenge the sentimental or psychological readings that Leigh and Trevelyan have advanced

questions.question: Daniel, you've described Magdalen's so-called redemption — the marriage to Kirke, the tearful moment over Norah's letter — as economic reabsorption into coverture. Collins gets her ill, gets her helpless, gets her dependent, and *rewards* her for it. But Edmund would say virtue here is circumstantially purchased, not morally earned. Are you two actually agreeing, or is there a real disagreement about what the novel thinks it's doing versus what it's actually doing?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Leigh's legal-philosophical account and Rosen's economic-materialist account — they reach similar conclusions about the 'redemption' being hollow but for different reasons; surface whether that's genuine agreement or a fundamental divergence in how they read Collins's intention

questions.question: Oliver, final push — because you've said something that I think the others might want to contest. You've argued the law doesn't *cause* Magdalen's breakdown; the law is just the only available language to describe something the novel already knows. Edmund would say the law is the *engine* of her destruction. Daniel would say it's the economic structure underneath the law. Who's right — and does it matter for how we read that last passage, where she 'victoriously tramples down' her jealousy over Norah's inheritance? Is 'trampled' triumph or self-amputation?
questions.intent: Close the segment by triangulating all three positions through the c56:p17 passage, which each expert reads differently — force Trevelyan to defend his most contentious claim and let Leigh and Rosen respond

steering_notes: This segment has genuine intellectual tension between three positions that *look* compatible but actually disagree about causation: Leigh says law creates the psychological void; Trevelyan says law is just the available vocabulary for a pre-legal psychological reality; Rosen says both are idealist mystifications and the real engine is economic. The host should resist letting them harmonise too quickly — the disagreement about the *redemption* passage (c56:p17) is the sharpest fault line and should be saved for the end. Keep the tone materialist and specific: when anyone drifts into abstraction, ask them to point back to the text. The Married Women's Property Act 1870 is useful context: Collins published in 1862, eight years before the Act — Rosen in particular may want to use this to argue Collins was diagnosing something Parliament hadn't yet named.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's claim that Magdalen's despair is economic rationality directly challenges Leigh's reading of her psychological dissolution as legally authorised — they should be pushed to say whether these are competing explanations or whether Leigh's legal argument requires Rosen's economic foundation to work

Trevelyan's reading of 'trampled' in c56:p17 as self-destruction disguised as virtue is almost identical to Leigh's claim that redemption is circumstantially purchased — but Leigh attributes this to legal restoration while Trevelyan attributes it to learned performance of feminine self-sacrifice; surface whether this is the same observation or a genuine disagreement about Collins's intent

segment_name: The Machinery of Plot: Collins's Narrative Architecture

questions.question: Daniel, you said something in our chat that's stuck with me — that the plot of *No Name* doesn't really belong to Magdalen, it belongs to the law. Can you unpack that? Because most readers experience this as Magdalen's story, her fight, her scheme — and you're saying that's almost an illusion Collins is engineering.
questions.intent: Establish Rosen's central thesis early and provocatively — that law is the true protagonist — which will immediately create tension with both Leigh's moral-order reading and Trevelyan's performative-voice reading

questions.question: Oliver, there's this extraordinary moment in the text — 'Any more letters from Miss Vanstone will be returned unopened' — and you described it as the plot machinery shifting from character action to pure administrative procedure. What does that sentence actually do to us as readers in the moment we hit it?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to articulate his strongest claim about syntax enacting powerlessness, and invite Rosen to respond on the legal-mechanism angle and Leigh on the moral scandal of it

questions.question: Edmund, both Oliver and Daniel have been treating the plot machinery as more or less value-neutral — it just grinds, it just excludes. But you think that's the scandal, don't you? That Collins is actually demolishing the idea that the legal order is just — and then at the end, he blinks. He rescues Magdalen anyway. Why is that rescue a problem rather than a comfort?
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's Johnsonian critique of the artificial redemption, set up a direct clash with Rosen who sees Magdalen as never truly agentive, and with Trevelyan who might see the ending as a vocal/syntactic restoration

questions.question: Oliver, I want to push on Wragge — because all three of you have flagged that line about carrying his head as high without a shirt-collar. You read it as dignity being a physical practice. Daniel reads it as compelled labour. Edmund thinks it might be moral self-deception. Are any of you wrong, or is Collins deliberately making that line do three things at once?
questions.intent: Create a direct three-way confrontation on a single passage — force the experts to account for each other's readings of the same sentence, generating productive disagreement

questions.question: Daniel, you pointed out that Collins marks two intestacies in a row with the word 'curiously' — as if systematic wealth transfer were sheer accident. Oliver would probably say that's a rhythmic and tonal move. Edmund would say it's moral evasion. What do you think Collins is actually doing by pretending not to see what he obviously sees?
questions.intent: Get Rosen to articulate authorial irony as structural concealment of legal mechanics, and invite the other two to disagree about whether Collins is exposing or participating in that concealment

steering_notes: This segment has strong potential for genuine three-way disagreement because all three experts are working from the same four passages and reaching incompatible conclusions about what the plot machinery *means*. The key fault line is whether Collins's narrative architecture is primarily formal (Trevelyan), moral-philosophical (Leigh), or economic-legal (Rosen). Push them toward the Wragge shirt-collar line and the 'letters returned unopened' sentence as shared battlegrounds — both passages appear in all three pre-interviews, so they're the natural collision points. The ending-as-editorial-rescue point (Leigh) is the most radioworthy provocation — save it for mid-segment when the conversation has enough momentum to sustain it. Keep the tone warm but let the disagreements land; this is a genuinely contested text.

segment_name: Between Deception and Desperation: Magdalen's Moral Arc

questions.question: Daniel, you've argued that Magdalen's deceptions aren't really moral failures — they're survival strategies generated by a legal system that essentially killed her as a person the moment her father died without marrying her mother. So when Edmund talks about Aristotelian vice and self-undermining schemes, is he even diagnosing the right patient? Is the novel actually about Magdalen's character, or about what the law did to her?
questions.intent: Establish the fundamental interpretive fault line early — moral agency vs structural determination — and provoke Edmund to defend his Aristotelian reading against a materialist challenge

questions.question: Edmund, you want to read that sunrise passage — 'the morning sun was warm on her face... and the sea was a sea of gold' — as the beginning of genuine moral awakening, but you're also insisting it isn't redemption yet, that she hasn't chosen anything. So what exactly is happening to Magdalen in that moment? Because Daniel thinks the golden sea is Collins aestheticising a woman who is basically facing the workhouse, and Oliver thinks the whole thing works through breath and rhythm rather than meaning at all.
questions.intent: Get Edmund to commit to a precise account of the sunrise passage, then surface the three-way disagreement about what that scene actually does — moral, economic, linguistic

questions.question: Oliver, you've said that Magdalen's moral state is actually audible — that by the time we reach that sunrise scene, her syntax has collapsed into something simpler, more regularised, and that a performer experiences that as restoration rather than reads it as restoration. What does that sound like? And does that linguistic collapse feel like freedom to you, or does it feel like defeat?
questions.intent: Draw out the performance-based reading of c39:p161 in concrete sensory terms and push Trevelyan toward the question of whether linguistic simplification is recovery or erasure of self

questions.question: Edmund, the father scene — he 'caught her round the waist, forced her, before she was aware of it, to look him in the face, and kissed her.' You call that the novel's tragic moment, the father teaching Magdalen that her impulses are noble. But Daniel is reading that same passage as the moment her body becomes the only asset she has left — legal property converted into physical possession. And Oliver hears the capitalized 'Me' a few pages earlier as Magdalen genuinely caught between feeling and strategy. Three of you, same scene, completely different Magdalens. Who's right?
questions.intent: Force a direct three-way collision on c10:p72 — the most contested passage in the pre-interviews — and let the disagreement run

questions.question: Daniel, let's end on George Bartram — 'there is only one woman in the world whom I can marry, and that woman is Miss Vanstone.' Edmund thinks that's the novel's moral hero: practical wisdom, grace beyond strict justice. But the Secret Trust you've been talking about restricts Magdalen's inheritance if she's a widow — which means Bartram's very proposal is also, structurally, the law releasing its grip on her only through a man's decision to marry her. Is that redemption, or is that the system working exactly as designed?
questions.intent: Close the segment by putting Edmund's moral reading and Daniel's structural reading in direct collision on the ending, leaving the audience with the unresolved tension rather than a tidy conclusion

steering_notes: This segment has a genuine three-way fault line that will do most of the work: Edmund's Aristotelian moral reading, Daniel's legal-materialist reading, and Oliver's linguistic-performative reading all converge on the same two or three passages (c10:p72 and c39:p161 above all) and produce completely different accounts of what those passages mean. The segment should end without resolution: the ending of the novel is genuinely contested among all three, and that's the right place to leave the audience.

questions.question: Oliver, there's a sentence Edmund flagged — 'In that instant he saw the woman whose beauty was the haunting remembrance of his life' — where Kirke recognises Magdalen outside her social position. questions.question: Daniel, you zeroed in on that line where Pendril tells the sisters they still have their father's 'legacy of repentance and love' — even though he's just told them they have no legal claim to a penny. You called that ideological cover for material abandonment. But isn't Collins asking us to feel the sincerity of that sentiment? What's he actually doing when he puts those words in Pendril's mouth?
questions.intent: Draw out Rosen's sharpest claim — that the novel launders legal dispossession through sentiment — and set up immediate pushback from Leigh, who reads Andrew's repentance as morally genuine

questions.question: Edmund, you'd push back on that pretty hard, I think. You've argued that this novel is fundamentally about morality being constructed rather than inherited — not just received from a father or conferred by a court. So when Pendril offers that emotional inheritance in place of the legal one, is that Collins exposing a con, or is it actually the novel's deepest moral claim?
questions.intent: Force Leigh to defend the affective and ethical weight of the consolation scene against Rosen's materialist reading, sharpening the disagreement

questions.question: Oliver, you've listened to both of those takes — and your argument is that we're all reading these passages too quietly. You said Pendril's line, the 'may help you in breaking the hard truth' sentence, performs legal powerlessness through its hedging and its tentative phrasing. If we heard that passage read aloud right now, what would we hear that the argument on the page can't give us?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to make the case for performance and rhythm as meaning — ideally triggering him to read or voice the passage — and create a moment of contrast with the purely thematic approaches of the other two

questions.question: Daniel, you flagged Wragge's account of how he makes money as the one moment in the novel that honestly describes how capital actually accumulates — inheritance from female relatives, swindling, commercial hustle — and you said it's only allowed to be honest because it's filtered through a comic character. Does that mean Collins knows exactly what he's doing and is hiding it in plain sight, or is the comedy a blind spot?
questions.intent: Push Rosen on whether Collins is complicit in the ideology or cannily subversive — and draw Leigh and Trevelyan into a three-way argument about authorial irony

questions.question: Edmund, here's the question I want to end on, because you said something in our pre-conversation that I haven't been able to shake: you said the ending isn't a restoration, it's a tragedy — no innocence is recoverable. But a lot of readers, and Victorian critics, read it as Collins ultimately rewarding Magdalen's reform and punishing her scheming. Who's right, and what does the answer tell us about what Collins actually believed justice looks like?
questions.intent: Crystallise the segment's central tension — between a conservative, reconciliatory reading and a tragic, irreversible one — and invite Rosen and Trevelyan to close with their own verdicts

steering_notes: This segment has a genuine three-way tension worth protecting. Leigh reads the novel as moral philosophy; Rosen reads it as ideology critique; Trevelyan reads it as performance and form. None of these are reconcilable without concession, so resist the urge to synthesise too early. Let Rosen and Leigh argue about Pendril's consolation speech for as long as it stays hot — that's the emotional core of the segment. Bring Trevelyan in as a disruptor when the argument goes purely thematic, since his move is always to say 'but listen to what the sentence is doing.' Watch for the moment when Rosen concedes (if he does) that Collins might be more self-aware than his ideology thesis allows — that's the segment's turning point. Keep the Wragge question loose enough that all three can chase it.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's claim that Pendril's consolation language is ideological cover directly contradicts Leigh's claim that the novel's moral philosophy is its deepest achievement — force them to argue about whether sentiment can substitute for material justice

Trevelyan's reading of Magdalen's urgency as rhythmically and syntactically distinct from legal authority complements Rosen's point about her rational response to structural dispossession — but Trevelyan frames it as epistemological visibility, Rosen frames it as economic rationality — get them to work out whether those are the same claim

Leigh reads the ending as tragedy with no restoration of innocence; Rosen reads it as the law's violence going unchallengeable; Trevelyan might read it as the prose's justice narrative exhausting itself — these three endings of the same novel are worth colliding explicitly in the final question

segment_name: A Name Reclaimed: Synthesis and the Novel's Radical Vision

questions.question: Daniel, you've said the marriage certificate in c13:p74 is basically the legal system working exactly as designed — not a twist, not a betrayal, just arithmetic. But that date, March the twentieth, eighteen forty-six — Collins makes it feel like a gut-punch. Does the novel earn that emotional weight, or is it dressing up a property transfer in sensation-novel clothing?
questions.intent: Open the central tension of the segment: is the novel's power moral, formal, or legal? Draw out Daniel's strongest materialist reading before the others can frame it differently.

questions.question: Oliver, you'd say the gut-punch is entirely in the prose — that the certificate passage is deliberately flat and bureaucratic, and that flatness *is* the argument. But Daniel is basically saying Collins is documenting a legal machine. Are those the same claim, or are you and Daniel actually disagreeing about where the novel's radicalism lives?
questions.intent: Force direct engagement between Oliver and Daniel — Oliver's formal argument about emotional temperature versus Daniel's materialist argument about legal mechanics. Set up productive disagreement.

questions.question: Edmund, you've got a different move here — you've argued that Magdalen's scheming fails, and that what she recovers at the end comes from outside her: Captain Kirke, Norah's marriage, grace from somewhere else. Daniel would say that's just the system closing around her. Oliver might say the prose already told us feeling was irrelevant. So who's right about what Collins is actually doing with that ending — is it moral growth, structural foreclosure, or something else?
questions.intent: Get Edmund's virtue-ethics reading into direct collision with Daniel's structuralist reading. The ending is where all three readings diverge most sharply — this is the productive disagreement.

questions.question: Edmund, you quoted that moment — 'There is nobody to speak for us, except — except me' — and called it the moment Magdalen has to become her own advocate by ceasing to be herself. Daniel hears it as eight words containing the entire structure of women's legal disability. Is that a contradiction, or are the two readings saying the same thing from opposite ends?
questions.intent: Create a moment of cross-engagement on a shared passage (c10:p64) where Edmund and Daniel have strikingly convergent but differently-framed readings. Let them find unexpected agreement or sharpen disagreement.

questions.question: Last one, and it's the big one. Winifred Hughes called sensation fiction a literature of anxiety about social instability. All three of you have been circling something like: Collins exposes the law as producing the very disorder it claims to prevent. Oliver, in a novel where documents are more powerful than people — where the prose refuses emotion because feeling is beside the point — can *No Name* actually have a radical vision, or does the flatness swallow it?
questions.intent: Close the segment with a synthesis question that pulls all three readings together. Give Oliver the formal-argument last word but leave space for Edmund and Daniel to complicate it. End on genuine uncertainty rather than resolution.

steering_notes: This segment is the synthesis, so let the disagreements that have been building come to a head — don't smooth them over. The three experts agree that the novel exposes something about law and women's property, but they disagree about *where* the radicalism lives: in the moral structure (Edmund), in the prose's formal refusal of emotion (Oliver), or in the documentary logic of property law (Daniel). The ending is the sharpest fault line — Edmund sees moral cost and grace, Daniel sees structural foreclosure, Oliver sees the prose already having made the argument before the plot resolves. Push toward that disagreement rather than away from it. Keep the tone of smart friends arguing in a pub — these are big ideas but they should feel urgent and personal, not academic.
cross_engagement_targets: Daniel and Oliver on c13:p74: Daniel reads the certificate as legal mechanics working as designed; Oliver reads its flat prose as a formal argument that documents replace human agency. These look like the same claim but have different implications — push them to identify the difference.

Edmund and Daniel on c10:p64: Both want to quote 'There is nobody to speak for us, except — except me' but for different reasons — Edmund for the cost to Magdalen's selfhood, Daniel for the legal structure it encodes. Get them to work out whether they are disagreeing or converging.

All three on the ending: Edmund sees external grace and moral cost; Daniel sees the triumph of the system and foreclosure of options; Oliver sees the prose as having already rendered feeling irrelevant. This is the segment's climax — make sure all three get to contest it directly.

Oliver vs Edmund on Magdalen's agency: Oliver argues her greatest power in c10:p64 is surrender; Edmund argues her agency fails and restoration comes from outside. These are close but not identical — Oliver is making a formal point about voice and constraint, Edmund a moral point about the limits of will.
